title: Chevron Is Doubling Venezuela Production. ExxonMobil Says It's Not in a Rush. Who's Right? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil remains cautious after Venezuela twice seized its assets. Uncertain long-term oil demand adds to investment risks. ExxonMobil's capital discipline could benefit long-term shareholders. Chevron(NYSE: CVX) plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years, potentially more than doubling its oil production there to about 600,000 barrels per day. ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), meanwhile, isn't interested in rushing back into Venezuela. And quite frankly, I think ExxonMobil may have the better strategy. Chevron isn't starting from scratch. The company has operated in Venezuela for more than a century and maintained a presence, even as political instability and economic turmoil have driven other international oil companies away. In fact, in September, Chevron announced agreements providing improved fiscal, commercial, and legal terms for its Venezuelan operations. It also secured additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Management believes it can expand production while keeping total costs below $20 per barrel. Indeed, that's a pretty attractive proposition. Chevron already has infrastructure, local relationships, and operating experience. Expanding existing production is considerably different from building an entirely new business in a country with Venezuela's history. And if oil prices remain favorable, Chevron could generate substantial additional cash flow without taking on the same level of risk as a newcomer. Exxon has good reasons to be skeptical. The company has had its Venezuelan assets seized twice, most recently in 2007 under former President Hugo Chávez. CEO Darren Woods has indicated that Exxon would consider returning, but only with stronger legal protections and investment terms that justify the risks. I don't blame him. Venezuela's oil infrastructure needs substantial investment, political uncertainty remains high, and there's no guarantee future governments will honor today's agreements. And there's also reason to consider long-term oil demand. There are varying projections on this. The IEA projects that global oil demand could plateau around 2030. Wood Mackenzie has that plateau hitting in 2032. TotalEnergies(NYSE: TTE) has it between 2035 and 2040, while OPEC suggests "robust global oil demand growth prospects to 2050, with no signs of oil demand peaking over the forecast period." But even with OPEC's optimistic scenario, 2050 is only about 23 years away. Of course, even if demand levels off, existing oil fields will continue declining. The industry will still need replacement production. But if demand growth slows while producers keep expanding capacity, oil prices could face additional pressure. Under these conditions, spending billions on politically risky projects becomes harder to justify. Chevron's expansion isn't necessarily a mistake. Its existing operations, relatively low production costs, and improved contractual terms could make Venezuela a profitable source of additional oil production. But ExxonMobil doesn't have the same advantages. It would potentially need to commit substantial capital to rebuild operations in a country that has already confiscated its assets. The company has other places to invest, including Guyana and the Permian Basin, where it has established operations and greater confidence in its ability to generate returns. Overall, ExxonMobil's strategy just makes sense. Yes, Chevron could make plenty of money in Venezuela. But ExxonMobil is demonstrating that having the financial resources to pursue an opportunity doesn't mean you should. Sometimes the better investment decision is knowing when to walk away. title: Buy Or Sell Energy Stocks After Their Worst Election Week? - Trefis
content: Here’s a tempting idea for the week after an election: buy whatever got hit hardest, because the crowd overreacted. There’s some real data behind it, and we’ll show you all of it, the wins and the losses. But the question that will serve you better is a quieter one: if energy or chips fell hard in your portfolio last week, does your plan already say what to do? We’ll come back to that at the end, after the numbers. “The headline sells the stock. Your plan decides whether you should.” – Anonymous That this was an odd election week. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% the day after the vote, then was down 2.5% by Friday’s close. Of the 11 elections since 2006, only 2006 had also gone up on day one and been down by day three, and then by just 0.1%. The election didn’t do that. On Thursday the S&P 500 fell 4.4% as the AI trade unwound, led by the chip makers and the companies building power and data centers for AI. The why: a growing backlash against data centers and open talk of bans and moratoriums, including a pledge from Texas’s governor-elect. The week’s biggest losers were the chip fund SMH, down 10.5%, the oil and gas producers fund XOP, down 9.3%, and the energy fund XLE, down 7.6%. For both energy funds it was the worst election week in our 20-year record. The winners: airlines (JETS), gold (GLD, its best election week on record) and communication services (XLC). Here is every election’s single worst fund over the three days, and what it did over the next twelve months, measured from the third day’s close: Six beat the S&P 500. The election week’s single best fund did it only 4 times in 10. The wins were real, and some were big. After the 2020 election, regional banks and oil producers were among the week’s losers; over the next year the regional bank fund rose 85% and XOP rose 179%, while the S&P 500 rose 34%. After 2016, utilities (XLU) fell 6.4% in the week and then rose 26%, beating the market. Clean energy fell 8% after both 2016 and 2024; it then rose 18%, about level with the S&P 500, and 46%, more than three times its gain. The losses were real too. In 2008 clean energy fell 18% in three days and was still down a year later, while the S&P 500 rose 17%. The bank fund KBE fell 13% that week and roughly another half over the next three months. A big fall can be the start of a bigger one. This is where we try to talk ourselves out of it. One fund per election is just 10 data points. So we counted the three worst and the five worst of each election week too, among the 22 sector and theme funds we checked, and set them beside the best: With the longer lists, the losers’ edge shrinks toward a coin flip. The winners lagged a bit more often than not. Across all those funds and elections, a fund’s election week against the S&P 500 pointed the same way as its next year less than half the time. The honest lesson: election week didn’t sort winners from losers. If anything, it nudged prices a little too far, a little too fast. Start with energy, since it had its worst week on record. The big oil companies went into the election as the market’s quiet winners of the past year, and they gave a slice of it back: A bad week inside a very good year. Exxon, Chevron and ConocoPhillips were at their 52-week closing highs on Oct 30. They aren’t priced for perfection. Price-to-earnings ratios run from about 7 for Marathon to about 17 for Exxon, and Chevron pays a 3.4% dividend. Revenue grew 13% to 31% over the past year. And what did energy do after its earlier losing election weeks? It’s a split decision: Two beat the market, two didn’t. Nothing to bet the house on either way. Then chips. SMH’s 10.5% drop is about level with 2008’s as the worst chip election week in 20 years, and SMH rose over the following year after all 10 earlier elections. But this year’s chip selloff was the AI trade, not the vote: worries about power and data-center opposition. Buyers tend to stay away until they have a clear reason to come back. Here’s the one we’d watch: an outright stop on data centers would hand the AI lead to China, and that isn’t happening. The spending is close to unstoppable. As we showed on Nov 5, Big Tech spent $1.15 for every $1 of cash it brought in last quarter, and even Nike has cut jobs while it keeps paying for AI. If losers deserve a second look, so do winners, since the single best fund of election week lagged the market 6 times in 10. Here’s how this year’s winners did after their previous best election weeks, all of which came in 2022: The S&P 500 rose 12.6% over the same 12 months. One of the four beat it. Newmont is the one to look at carefully. It’s up about 50% in a year and more than tripled in three, trades at about 14 times earnings, and its operating margin over the past year was more than double its five-year average. That’s a business riding a high gold price. It’s also a stock already near the top of its range, about 7% below its high. Put energy and gold side by side and the week tells two stories at once. Energy falling while airlines rise is what you’d expect with oil getting cheaper (the oil fund USO fell 6% in the week), which would cool inflation. Gold having its best election week on record is what you’d expect if investors wanted protection, from inflation or from a shaky market. Long Treasuries edged up 1%, so long rates eased a little. Markets are hedging both ways. The Labor Department’s October consumer price report is due today, Tuesday, Nov 10. Why would anyone want that protection? Our October case was that inflation is back, driven by three words, war, immigration and taxes, with AI spending as a fourth fuel on the fire: Inflation Is Back. Is A Stock Market Crash Next? None of those four went away on election night. That’s why gold drew buyers, and it’s what would bring buyers back to energy: if oil’s dip proves short and inflation stays sticky, energy’s bad week looks like a pause in a strong year. If inflation really cools, gold’s best week is the one more likely to fade. That’s the useful part for a long-run investor. Energy and gold are your inflation insurance. Selling the insurance because it had a bad week, or doubling it because it had a good one, is how a plan gets turned upside down by three trading days. Over the 10 earlier elections, the S&P 500 rose in the 12 months after day three every single time, by 2% to 34%. The losers’ list kept changing: clean energy, health care, banks, Treasuries, biotech. What didn’t change is that the market as a whole went up over the year that followed. The part that will still matter in 2027 is how much of each sector you hold and why, not which one had the worst Thursday. 1. Check your energy and gold weights against your plan. Energy’s fall and gold’s rise both moved your mix a little. If either is now outside the band you set, rebalance back. If you never set one, set it now. 2. Don’t sell a loser because it lost. Sell it if the reason you own it changed. Exxon is still the business it was two weeks ago. 3. Don’t buy a loser just because it lost. The 2008 clean-energy case shows the risk. If you want more energy or chips, add in pieces, on a schedule, with a size you’d be fine holding through another 20% fall. 4. Write down when you’ll look again. Three months, not three days. Our one-page plan for the whole portfolio is in Will Stocks Rebound Today, Or Do You Have A Plan? What this replaces: dumping last week’s losers, or loading up on them because “losers bounce.” The risk: if oil keeps falling, energy stocks can keep falling with it, and a plan won’t stop that. It keeps you from making a five-year decision on a three-day chart. Losers bounced a bit more often than winners, but not reliably. The single worst fund of election week beat the S&P 500 over the next year 6 times in 10; widen to the five worst and it’s 28 in 50, not far from a coin flip. This year’s losers, energy and chips, fell for reasons that started outside the election: the AI trade, and energy giving back part of a very strong year. Treat energy and gold as the inflation insurance in your plan, rebalance by your band, and look again in three months. Follow this story with us: we’ll score this year’s losers and winners against the record in three months and again in a year. One week rarely decides a year. title: Should You Buy Exxon Mobil Stock For Its Cash? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Exxon Mobil (XOM) produced free cash flow equal to 6.3% of its market value over the last twelve months, against 4.2% for the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high marks either a business on sale or one that investors expect to earn less, and which side Exxon is on depends on whether its refineries and oil fields keep making that cash once today’s fuel shortage eases. So how steady has Exxon’s cash been? Exxon Mobil’s Cash Has Swung Widely But Stayed Positive Exxon’s free cash flow stayed above zero in every twelve-month stretch ending between September 2023 and September 2026, ranging from $18.8 billion to $43.0 billion. Shareholders own a slice of that cash whether the company pays it out or keeps it, just as they own a share of its profit. When investors give that cash its full value, the share price tends to follow, and more so while the cash is growing. Exxon runs about 3.6 million barrels of crude a day through its refineries, management said on its October 30 call, and it produces oil in the Permian and Guyana. Over the last twelve months, the company put 39.1% of the cash its operations brought in back into capital spending, leaving the rest as free cash. Little of that cash has to go to lenders first. Exxon ended September with $22.1 billion in net debt, or total debt minus cash, which amounted to 3.2% of its market value. Operating income covered its interest expense 55.6 times over the last twelve months. Exxon produced $35.5 billion, or most of its twelve-month free cash flow, in its two latest quarters, fiscal Q2 and Q3 2026. Management said that during the third quarter, conflict in the Middle East constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline, which left markets short and prices higher. Before that, Exxon’s sales had been falling. Revenue fell 4.4% in the twelve months to September 2025, after a 1.8% fall the year before. In the year to September 2025, free cash flow dropped to $23.8 billion from $32.8 billion. Exxon’s price appears to assume that much of the cash it made in 2026 will fade as the shortage eases. Management credits part of the 2026 gain to its own work, saying earlier investments that raised diesel output added $3.5 billion of margins so far in 2026, and management also counts $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019 on the way to $20 billion by 2030. Exxon’s U.S. Gulf Coast projects, starting at Baytown, are expected to raise output of distillates, such as diesel, by about 100,000 barrels a day. Management said on its call that it has no clear view of how long fuel markets will stay short. Its best guess was that markets will take until well into 2027 to get closer to normal, and possibly longer. The debt is the smaller question, since Exxon lowered its net debt by more than $9 billion in the third quarter, management said. Exxon’s cash has come through past swings with little debt ahead of its owners, but whether the higher cash of 2026 outlasts the shortage is still open. Exxon’s free cash flow in its fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch.
